content_list.content_text: The Vietnam War was the first war of the television age and produced striking images of the harsh reality of the battlefield. In contrast to World War II, however, Hollywood showed a distinct lack of enthusiasm for producing patriotic films. Usually cited as the only pro-war feature produced during the conflict, The Green Berets (1968) was savaged by critics for its simplistic stance.

information.contentText: Based on Oliver Stone's personal experience in the Vietnam War, the film shows the horrors of the conflict through the eyes of Chris Taylor, a young American recruit who volunteers for combat. In the war, the young man comes into contact with Sergeants Bob Barnes and Elias Grodin: the former a brutal, psychopathic killer; the latter an intelligent, sensitive pacifist. Starring Charlie Sheen, Tom Berenger, Willem Dafoe and a large cast, the film's screenplay was written by Oliver Stone himself and was completed around 1976.

content_list.content_text: Hollywood films of the late 1960s and early 1970s tended to offer less direct reflections on the war. The insolent, anti-authoritarian tone of M*A*S*H (1970) had more to do with Vietnam than with its supposed setting, the Korean War. Ulzana's Raid (1972), a fascinating Western by Robert Aldrich (1918-1983), uses the story of a cavalry troop with the unhappy mission of recapturing a band of Apaches as a metaphor for a war that cannot be won.

Authentic dramatizations of the Vietnam War had to wait until the fighting was over. In 1978, Coming Home (1978), by Hal Ashby (1928-1988), criticized the war through the misadventures of a disabled veteran. Released the same year, The Deer Hunter (1978), by Michael Cimino (b. 1939), was more ambiguous in its attitude. Although described as an antiwar film, it was harshly criticized for presenting a brutal and one-sided image of the North Vietnamese.

information.contentText: The film was loosely inspired by the book Three Comrades (1937), by World War I veteran Erich Maria Remarque, author of Im Westen nichts Neues, which tells the story of three World War I veterans in the Weimar Republic. As in the book, The Deer Hunter explores the moral and mental consequences of the violence of war and of patriotism politically manipulated through honor, friendship and family, in a small, close-knit rural community. The film deals with controversial subjects such as drug abuse, infidelity and mental illness.

content_list.content_text: The Russian roulette scene in particular stirred controversy, as there was no evidence whatsoever that the North Vietnamese had used the deadly game. It was Apocalypse Now (1979), made by Francis Ford Coppola (b. 1939) the following year, that provided the most powerful and enduring creation of the Vietnam experience and set a standard by which all other films on the subject came to be judged.

content_list.title: Platoon
content_list.description:
Writer-director Oliver Stone (b. 1946) was the first Vietnam veteran to get Hollywood backing to make an autobiographical film about the conflict. The Deer Hunter (1978) and Apocalypse Now (1979) had turned the war into subject matter for movies, but it was Platoon that showed the reality of Vietnam to generations who only came of age after the conflict was over.

Chris Taylor (Charlie Sheen), who stands in for Stone, is an idealistic young man who volunteered to serve with the infantry in Vietnam. He feels torn between two "fathers": the gentle, sensitive super-soldier Sergeant Elias (Willem Dafoe), who smokes pot and listens to soul with the Black soldiers, and the sadistic, scar-faced Sergeant Barnes (Tom Berenger), who drinks and listens to country and western with the rednecks. Chris follows the path of other screen soldiers, "becoming a man", but whereas the recruits whipped into shape by John Wayne always ended up saluting the flag, Chris ends up losing faith in his country amid the blood and confusion.

Although it is overly schematic in pitting the two sergeants against each other and contrasting their philosophies, Platoon is a powerful film. Terrifying as he is, Barnes teaches Chris how to survive rather than become a martyr - the climax, unthinkable in earlier films, has Chris shooting one of his own superiors rather than facing the enemy. Harrowing and suspenseful as it is, the film is not devoid of nostalgia - the soundtrack is made up of big 1960s hits and, in one scene, the soldiers sing "The Tracks of My Tears" by Smokey Robinson & The Miracles.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Kim Newman, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

content_list.content_text: Films dealing with America's emotional landscape in the wake of Vietnam provided an oblique commentary on the war. Who'll Stop the Rain (1976) shows a veteran and his best friend's wife on the trail of a shipment of Vietnamese heroin in California. The madness of the war is encapsulated in one of the film's lines of dialogue: "You see, in a world where elephants are pursued by flying men, people naturally want to get high."

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme Nascido para Matar
information.contentText: The plot follows a platoon of U.S. Marines through their training at the Marine Corps Recruit Depot in South Carolina, focusing mainly on two privates, Joker and Pyle, who struggle under their abusive, hard-line drill instructor, Sergeant Hartman, and on the experiences of two of the platoon's Marines in the Vietnamese cities of Da Nang and Huế during the Tet Offensive at the height of the Vietnam War.

content_list.content_text: Oliver Stone (b. 1946) drew on his experience in Vietnam to make Platoon (1986), the first of a trilogy depicting different aspects of the war. The second, Born on the Fourth of July (1989), was based on the memoir of a disabled war veteran, and the third, Heaven & Earth (1993), is the true story of a young Vietnamese woman who marries a traumatized soldier.

Stanley Kubrick (1928-1999) created an intense vision of Vietnam when he rebuilt the battlefields of Southeast Asia in the marshes east of London to shoot Full Metal Jacket (1987). The conflict in Vietnam spilled across the borders into Cambodia when the Americans left in 1975.

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme Pecados de Guerra
information.contentText: The film was based on a true case, known as the "Incident on Hill 192," and on Daniel Lang's book of the same title, but all the names and some details of the story were changed.

content_list.content_text: More than three million Cambodians were killed by the Khmer Rouge regime, as dramatized in the British film The Killing Fields (1984). It chronicles the barbaric events of Year Zero from the perspective of two journalists - one Cambodian, Dith Pran (Haing S. Ngor), and the other from New York, Sydney Schanberg (Sam Waterston) - including Pran's struggle to survive and his escape from one of the tortuous forced labor camps.

In the 21st century, attitudes toward Vietnam were reflected in a new political context. Made in the first year of the Iraq War, We Were Soldiers (2002), starring Mel Gibson (b. 1956), offers a sympathetic view of American intervention.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Dominic Power, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

content_list.content_text: How can a shoot planned for 16 weeks end up lasting 15 months? In the case of Apocalypse Now, the real feat is that (almost) every member of the crew managed to finish the job alive. Its director, Francis Ford Coppola, ended up following his protagonist, Captain Willard, in his plunge into madness: if the soldier's mission was to hunt down Colonel Kurtz, Coppola's was to finish a film he had started without a screenplay and without an ending. He himself would admit to having contemplated suicide on three occasions over the four years of production, when everything that could go wrong went wrong. And everything nobody had even imagined could happen turned out even worse.
content_list.content_title: ‘Apocalypse Now’:  the wildest set in history

information.contentText: The film has been noted for the problems encountered in making it. These problems were chronicled in the documentary Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse (1991) by Eleanor Coppola (b. 1936), which tells the story of Brando arriving on set overweight and completely unprepared; expensive sets being destroyed by bad weather; and its lead actor (Sheen) suffering a heart attack while on location. Problems continued after production, as the release was postponed several times while Coppola edited the footage thousands of times. It took about three and a half years to complete and in the end ran far over its estimated budget, since the shoot had fallen badly behind schedule.

content_list.content_text: No Hollywood studio wanted to hear about a film on Vietnam just months after the United States' defeat in the most controversial war in its history. Coppola secured the backing of the distributor United Artists, founded by Charles Chaplin (1889-1977) in 1930 so that artists would not have to depend on the commercial studios, but he was forced to negotiate personally with investors and back every loan with all his properties and the revenue still being generated by The Godfather (1972) and its sequel. In the '70s, Hollywood studios had not yet been absorbed by multinationals, so every dollar had to be negotiated. And shoots, thanks to the fact that executives were cinephiles rather than economists, could run long if the film deserved it.

information.contentTitle: Scene with the famous line "I love the smell of napalm in the morning"
information.contentText: Bill Kilgore's scene and monologue, "... I love the smell of napalm in the morning ...", is one of the most iconic in film history. Upon its release, Apocalypse Now won widespread critical acclaim, and its cultural impact and philosophical themes have been widely discussed ever since. Today it is widely regarded as one of the greatest films of all time.

content_list.content_text: Apocalypse Now (released in the summer of 1979) was, according to cinematographer Vittorio Storaro (b. 1940), "a picture of the imposition of one culture on another and of the Americans' desire to turn everything into a spectacle": if real soldiers played rock and roll while bombing Vietnamese villages, the ones in the film listened to Wagner's Ride of the Valkyries. If the army devastated Vietnam with napalm explosions, Coppola would film the biggest explosion ever produced outside a war. With a budget of 11 million dollars (the same amount as Star Wars (1977)), Apocalypse Now would be the first art-house blockbuster.

Steve McQueen (1930-1980) turned down the lead role, as did Al Pacino (b. 1940), Robert Redford (b. 1936) and Jack Nicholson (b. 1937). Frustration led Coppola to throw his five Oscars out the window and, after putting them back on the shelf, to hire Harvey Keitel (b. 1939). After three weeks of shooting, however, he realized that the actor's acting style did not suit a character who was supposed to function as a passive spectator on a journey to the end of the world and of the human soul. The replacement was Martin Sheen (b. 1940), who landed in the Philippines in the middle of his own battle with his demons: he drank nonstop, smoked three packs a day and, in one of the first scenes, collapsed on the floor screaming through tears. When he looked in the mirror and punched his reflection, his arm was covered in blood, but Coppola ordered the cameras to keep rolling while the actor screamed. Apocalypse Now had only just begun. The horror had not yet arrived.

information.contentText: Part of the huge set that had to be built in the Philippines to shoot ‘Apocalypse Now’.

content_list.content_text: Instead of working from a screenplay, Coppola carried everywhere a copy of Heart of Darkness (the unadaptable Joseph Conrad novel on which the film is based) that he had underlined. And he wrote each scene the night before. The production was made in the Philippines because the country's president, the dictator Ferdinand Marcos, made everything easier: in exchange for thousands of dollars a day, the crew could use Philippine army helicopters and pilots and bomb as many hectares of forest with napalm as it needed. But on several occasions the helicopters, cameras still running, abandoned the scene because they had to go fight the Filipino rebel guerrillas.

Coppola and his 900 workers had no choice but to wait, arms folded, for the pilots to wipe out the enemy and decide to return to the set. Often, the airmen who took part in the rehearsals were not the same ones who later showed up for the shoot, so everything had to start from scratch each morning. Like the Vietnam War itself, this shoot was the imposition of one culture on another (the sets were built by locals, exploited at one dollar a day, and one of them died buried under a block). And, as also happened with the Viet Cong, the invasion was not as easy as the Americans had thought.

information.contentText: Coppola explained that he had shot the now-iconic footage during the demolition of the sets (the destruction of the sets and their removal, as demanded by the Philippine government). He filmed the demolition with multiple cameras loaded with different film stocks and lenses to capture the explosions at different speeds. He wanted to do something with the dramatic images and decided to add them to the credits.

content_list.content_text: Typhoon Olga ravaged the Philippines in May 1976. Coppola tried to incorporate the rain into the film (monsoons battered Vietnam during the war), but the plan proved impractical when the storm destroyed several of the film's sets. On hearing this, the director reacted by cooking a nice plate of pasta while listening to Puccini's La Bohème. After dinner, he decided to halt shooting for two months. When he resumed, he ran straight into another force of nature: Marlon Brando (1924-2004).

Brando showed up weighing 130 kilos (even though the screenplay described Kurtz as a mythological, slender and athletic creature), without having read the screenplay and with no intention of sharing a scene with Dennis Hopper (1936-2010) - who, to build his character, had asked for 25 grams of cocaine, paid for out of the production budget. But Brando had every intention of collecting his salary of three million dollars for three weeks.

quote.quote: Francis wanted the sounds to be accurate, in high-fidelity stereo, and when someone fired an AK-47, it had to be an AK-47 with real bullets in it. We managed to get hold of those weapons and ammunition, and we went to a remote location where we could record and make original recordings with all the right perspectives.
quote.author: Walter Murch on the process of building the film's sound

content_list.content_text: Coppola had to postpone the shoot yet another week to read Brando's dialogue aloud and prepare the scenes with him. The filmmaker let the star improvise philosophical, martial and philanthropic reflections in an 18-minute monologue shot in shadow at the actor's request, as he did not want his physical bulk to distract viewers. He even put an earpiece in Brando's ear to feed him his lines. One day, Brando told Coppola that he had already used him enough and that, if he wanted more scenes, he should hire someone else. He got up from his chair, left and never appeared on the set again.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Marlon Brando's famous monologue
information.contentText: Marlon Brando as Colonel Walter E. Kurtz, whom Willard must kill. Brando arrived on set obese and fought with Coppola, refusing to read the screenplay. After a few days he supposedly read the book, shaved his head and decided to shoot his scenes.

content_list.content_text: While waiting for Brando to be ready, producer Gray Frederickson began to smell something rotten on the set of Kurtz's compound. "You have to get rid of the dead rats," he told production designer Dean Tavoularis, who explained that the rodents were there on purpose to create atmosphere. Suddenly, a prop man walking by exclaimed: "Just wait until you find the human corpses." To the producer's astonishment, they took him to a tent full of dead bodies, stored until Coppola was ready to shoot Willard's arrival at the compound (where there would be corpses hanging from the trees and strewn across the ground). "It's going to look really authentic," the designer promised.

The man who supplied the corpses did not work at a morgue, as he had claimed; he had stolen the bodies from graves. The police then shut down the production for several days to question each of the workers and make sure they were not murderers. Since it was impossible to return the unidentified bodies to their graves (and United Artists refused to pay for burials), nobody knows, or nobody has wanted to tell, what was done with them.

On March 5, 1977, four days after the shoot passed the one-year mark, Martin Sheen woke up at two in the morning with unbearable chest pain. The actor left his tent and dragged himself along the road, in agony, for a kilometer until he found help. He was having a heart attack. When he heard, Coppola suffered an epileptic seizure, but he tried to hide the incident from United Artists. "Even if Martin dies, he's not dead until I say so," the director warned. Coppola had run up a debt equivalent to 135 million reais that would have left his wife Eleanor and his three children (Gio, 12; Roman, 10; and Sofia, 4) destitute. Suicide was no longer even an option.

information.contentText: Problems arose again when Marcos and his air force began charging Coppola a fortune to rent helicopters, yet at the same time the generals seemed to regard the film as "a free pilot training program," wrote Michael Goodwin and Naomi Wise in On the Edge: The Life and Times of Francis Coppola. They sent a different group of rookie airmen every day, so the previous day's flight rehearsals were useless; thousands of dollars were lost.

content_list.content_text: Apocalypse Now, with a budget that today would be comparable to that of Venom (2018) or San Andreas (2015), had surpassed Cleopatra (1963) as the most expensive film in history up to that point. During the six weeks Sheen was out, Coppola shot scenes that were not in the screenplay, sent a telegram to his friend (and the project's original director) George Lucas (b. 1944) congratulating him on the success of Star Wars – and, while he was at it, asking for money – and kept stalling on finishing the film. As with war, Coppola knew when and how to start it (though never why), but had no idea how or when he would end it. And no matter how long he dragged it out, the ending would be there, waiting for him.

The final stage of the shoot was led by a Francis Ford Coppola who was 50 kilos lighter and insisted on pressing ahead despite the warning signs. The workers had dysentery almost daily, the actor who played the surfer Lance (Sam Bottoms) was always high on speed, marijuana or LSD because the whole crew partied until dawn, wild animals prowled around the camp tents at night, animal rights groups had denounced the slaughter of a water buffalo for the filming of the final scene, and United Artists intended to reduce the value of Coppola's life insurance. His life was no longer worth as much as at the start of the Apocalypse Now venture, but the film had to be finished even if it was (literally) the last thing he did. Only then would the investment be justified to the creditors. By this point, Coppola was already convinced the film would be astonishing.

quote.quote: There were never five endings, only one, even if there were differently edited versions.
quote.author: Richard Beggs on the rumors of the film's five endings

content_list.content_text: When he presented it at the Cannes Film Festival, where it would go on to win the Palme d'Or despite being unfinished, Coppola drew a parallel between the shoot and the war it depicted: "We were guys with access to too much money and too much equipment, and little by little we went insane. My film is not about Vietnam; my film is Vietnam."

information.contentText: Coppola and Roos had been impressed by Martin Sheen's screen test for the role of Michael Corleone in The Godfather, and he became their top choice to play Willard, but the actor had already accepted another project, and Harvey Keitel was cast in the role based on his work in Martin Scorsese's Mean Streets. Filming began three weeks later. Within a few days, Coppola was unhappy with Harvey Keitel's takes as the Captain, saying the actor "found it difficult to play him as a passive onlooker." After seeing the first scenes, the director flew back to Los Angeles and replaced Keitel with Sheen.

content_list.content_text: Apocalypse Now grossed five times its budget, which saved Coppola from bankruptcy, although his definitive ruin would come with One from the Heart (1982). Today, he says all the money he has is thanks to his vineyard in Napa, California. "The film isn't so strange anymore, seen today," the director reflected in 2019. "The same thing happened to it that happens to those avant-garde paintings that, over time, turn into wallpaper patterns."

Marlon Brando, until the last day of his life (he died in 2004), complained that Coppola was "a fat bastard" who owed him two million euros (9 million reais). Apocalypse Now took so long to shoot that, in 1978, The Deer Hunter stole its honor of being the first Hollywood film about Vietnam. Before handing the Oscar to the director of The Deer Hunter, Michael Cimino (who would ruin his career two years later, also bringing about the closure of United Artists, with Heaven's Gate (1980)), Coppola took the opportunity to issue a warning about Hollywood that was met with scorn: the press ridiculed him, concluding that he had gone definitively mad because of the Apocalypse Now shoot. What was the aberration Coppola dared to prophesy? "Get ready, because digital technology is about to change cinema forever."
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "40 years of ‘Apocalypse Now’: this was the wildest set in history," by Juan Sanguino on brasil.elpais.com.br.

movies.title: Apocalypse Now
movies.overview: At the height of the Vietnam war, Captain Benjamin Willard is sent on a dangerous mission that, officially, "does not exist, nor will it ever exist." His goal is to locate - and eliminate - a mysterious Green Beret Colonel named Walter Kurtz, who has been leading his personal army on illegal guerrilla missions into enemy territory.

movies.title: Platoon
movies.overview: As a young and naive recruit in Vietnam, Chris Taylor faces a moral crisis when confronted with the horrors of war and the duality of man.

movies.title: M*A*S*H
movies.overview: The staff of a Korean War field hospital use humor and high jinks to keep their sanity in the face of the horror of war.

movies.title: The Deer Hunter
movies.overview: A group of working-class friends decide to enlist in the Army during the Vietnam War and finds it to be hellish chaos -- not the noble venture they imagined. Before they left, Steven married his pregnant girlfriend -- and Michael and Nick were in love with the same woman. But all three are different men upon their return.

movies.title: Full Metal Jacket
movies.overview: A pragmatic U.S. Marine observes the dehumanizing effects the U.S.-Vietnam War has on his fellow recruits from their brutal boot camp training to the bloody street fighting in Hue.

movies.title: The Killing Fields
movies.overview: The real-life story of a friendship between two journalists, an American and a Cambodian, during the bloody Khmer Rouge takeover of Cambodia in 1975, which led to the death of 2-3 million Cambodians during the next four years, until Pol Pot's regime was toppled by the intervening Vietnamese in 1979.

movies.title: Hearts and Minds
movies.overview: Many times during his presidency, Lyndon B. Johnson said that ultimate victory in the Vietnam War depended upon the U.S. military winning the "hearts and minds" of the Vietnamese people. Filmmaker Peter Davis uses Johnson's phrase in an ironic context in this anti-war documentary, filmed and released while the Vietnam War was still under way, juxtaposing interviews with military figures like U.S. Army Chief of Staff William C. Westmoreland with shocking scenes of violence and brutality.

movies.title: Cutter's Way
movies.overview: Richard spots a man dumping a body, and decides to expose the man he thinks is the culprit with his friend Alex Cutter.

movies.title: Casualties of War
movies.overview: During the Vietnam War, a soldier finds himself the outsider of his own squad when they unnecessarily kidnap a female villager. Based on the actual events of an incident on Hill 192 in November, 1966.

movies.title: The Green Berets
movies.overview: Col. Mike Kirby picks two teams of crack Green Berets for two missions in South Vietnam. The first is to strengthen a camp that is trying to be taken by the enemy. The second is to kidnap a North Vietnamese General.

movies.title: Coming Home
movies.overview: The wife of a Marine serving in Vietnam, Sally Hyde decides to volunteer at a local veterans hospital to occupy her time. There she meets Luke Martin, a frustrated wheelchair-bound vet who has become disillusioned with the war. Sally and Luke develop a friendship that soon turns into a romance.

movies.title: Good Morning, Vietnam
movies.overview: Radio funny man Adrian Cronauer is sent to Vietnam to bring a little comedy back into the lives of the soldiers. After setting up shop, Cronauer delights the G.I.s but shocks his superior officer, Sergeant Major Dickerson, with his irreverent take on the war. While Dickerson attempts to censor Cronauer's broadcasts, Cronauer pursues a relationship with a Vietnamese girl named Trinh, who shows him the horrors of war first-hand.

movies.original_title: Born on the Fourth of July
movies.title: Born on the Fourth of July
movies.overview: The biography of Ron Kovic. Paralyzed in the Vietnam war, he becomes an anti-war and pro-human rights political activist after feeling betrayed by the country he fought for.

movies.title: Heaven & Earth
movies.overview: Le Ly lives in a small Vietnamese village whose serenity is shattered when war breaks out. Caught between the Viet Cong and the South Vietnamese army, the village is all but destroyed. After being both brutalized and raped, Le Ly resolves to flee. She leaves for the city, surviving desperate situations, but surviving nonetheless. Eventually she meets a U.S. Marine named Steve Butler who treats her kindly and tells her he would like to be married -- maybe to her.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1970 to 1989
content_list.description: The Exorcist is released, making audiences around the world sick and causing them to faint, creating a global hysteria. The first blockbuster is released: Jaws; meanwhile, auteur cinema grows with Martin Scorsese and other great directors. The '80s arrive with low-budget productions and era-defining comedies. Click here to see, in chronological order, the main events in cinema between 1940 and 1959.
